conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the neurology team doctors. You're here today for your scheduled high-dose methotrexate and rituximab treatment, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It’s my eleventh cycle, I believe. I’ve been feeling well since the last one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches your record. You’ve been doing well overall. Any new symptoms—headaches, vision changes, weakness, or fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing new. Just the same floaters in both eyes. They’ve been there for years and haven’t changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. Those are stable and not concerning at this point. We’ll monitor them. Any nausea, dizziness, or trouble with urination?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None of that. I’m feeling pretty normal, actually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll do a quick physical exam now and get your labs checked. Then we’ll start the infusion this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable—blood pressure 120 over 87, heart rate 79. You’re alert, no neurological deficits. Reflexes are normal, gait is steady. Everything looks good for treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was a little worried after last time when my liver enzymes went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that. But it resolved quickly with extra leucovorin and fluids. This time, we’re being extra cautious—we’ll keep you well-hydrated and use sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the rituximab—do I need pre-meds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you dexamethasone and Benadryl before the infusion to prevent any reaction. You tolerated it well last time, so we expect the same today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the methotrexate infusion. Dose is 6 grams per square meter, as planned. It’ll run over the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I expect to feel anything during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people don’t feel much during the infusion. Some get mild fatigue or nausea later. We have anti-nausea meds ready if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is going smoothly. You’re doing well. We’ll start leucovorin later tonight to help clear the methotrexate from your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How often will you check my levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your methotrexate blood levels every 12 to 24 hours until they drop to a safe level—below 0.1 micromolar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually by day four or five. We’ll keep you hydrated and monitor your urine pH to make sure your kidneys are protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRI from this morning shows no changes—no new lesions or signs of lymphoma recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. The old spot in the frontal lobe—is that still there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s unchanged—likely old blood or calcification. No enhancement, so no active disease. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my methotrexate level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 2.3 micromolar yesterday evening. This morning it’s down to 0.43. That’s a good drop—on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m clearing it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll keep giving leucovorin and fluids. Your kidney function is stable—creatinine is 0.9, which is normal for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest methotrexate level is 0.12 micromolar—almost at the target. We’ll give one more dose of leucovorin and stop the bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m almost done with the clearance phase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll check one final level tomorrow morning. If it’s below 0.1, you’ll be ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my eye floaters? Should I see the ophthalmologist again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re stable and not active lymphoma. Genteal eye drops can help with dryness or irritation, but no urgent need to see them unless they change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my aspirin—I should keep taking that daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your 81 mg aspirin. It’s for cardiovascular protection, especially with your family history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level this morning is 0.13 micromolar. That’s low enough. We’ll discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Do I need more leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with a few more doses—just to be safe. Take them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when’s my next follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In two weeks with your oncologist. They’ll review your progress and plan the next cycle if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any signs of the lymphoma coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The MRI showed no new enhancement or lesions. Your neurological exam is stable. That’s exactly what we want to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys—they’re okay after the methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, creatinine is normal, and your urine output has been good. No signs of tubular necrosis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. That was scary last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. You’re doing well. Just keep drinking fluids at home and watch for any unusual symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What medications should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your daily aspirin and multivitamin. Use Genteal drops if your eyes feel dry. And finish the leucovorin as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel unwell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or severe nausea. Otherwise, see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. Stay well, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge summary is ready. You’re being discharged in stable condition after completing your chemotherapy cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. Your oncologist will coordinate the next steps based on your response to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hyperlipidemia—I should keep watching my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue heart-healthy habits. Your lipid levels are being monitored as part of your overall care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well, Mr. Thompson. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will be in shortly with your discharge instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you at your follow-up.
